passage: Twenty minutes before the school bus left, the annual-day hall was still full of paint cans, and a power cut had switched off the fans. Everyone crowded round Sumitra's backdrop of snow peaks. "Unreal!" "Sumitra, do mine next!" Mridul stood behind them holding a brush over the blank welcome banner. He felt invisible, and his jaw tightened. "She probably traced it" rose to his tongue, but he shut his mouth on it. Why did it sting so much? Because he wanted someone to say wow to him. He knelt on the floor and began the big curly letters he had practised all term at the back of his notebook. When the bus horn sounded, the teacher stopped at the banner. "Who did this lettering?"

qa.q: Why were the fans off in the hall?
qa.a: There had been a power cut.

qa.q: Why did Mridul nearly say that Sumitra traced the backdrop?
qa.a: He felt invisible and stung by all the praise, so part of him wanted to bring Sumitra down, but he shut his mouth on it.

qa.q: What did Mridul do with his envy that helped him?
qa.a: He asked himself why it stung, saw that he wanted to be noticed for his own work, and put his effort into the lettering.

qa.q: What would change if Mridul had said the traced remark aloud?
qa.a: Sumitra would likely have felt hurt, and Mridul's own lettering might have gone unnoticed behind an argument.

grounding: Shows envy at a classmate's praised talent, felt as invisibility, turned into work on one's own strength instead of running the classmate down.

passage:
At the village school's Independence Day fair, everyone crowded round Kashish's rangoli: a peacock in twelve colours. The headmaster clapped. The teachers took photos. "Kashish is so talented," people kept saying.
Hafsa stood at the edge, holding the small clay lamp she had made. Nobody looked at it. She felt invisible. A mean thought crept up: her mother probably helped her.
She almost said it aloud to her friend. Then she stopped. That wasn't fair, and it wasn't even why she felt bad. She felt bad because she wanted to be noticed too.
That evening Hafsa told Nani. "What do you love doing?" Nani asked. "Telling stories," Hafsa said. So Nani helped her write one down, and the next week Hafsa read it at assembly. The whole class laughed in all the right places.

qa.q: What was Hafsa really feeling at the fair?
qa.a: Envious and invisible; she wanted to be noticed too.

qa.q: How did Hafsa turn her envy into something useful?
qa.a: She stopped herself from running Kashish down and worked on her own strength, storytelling.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt if Hafsa had said her mother helped?
qa.a: Hurt and unfairly accused, when she had done nothing wrong.

grounding: A girl who feels invisible while a classmate's talent is praised notices her envy and works on her own strength instead of running the classmate down.

passage:
In Wanjiru's class in Lisbon, everyone talked about Ines. Ines had played piano at the school concert, and the video was going round every parent's phone. Even Wanjiru's own mother watched it twice.
Wanjiru felt invisible. At recess she heard herself say, "She only plays well because she has lessons every day," and the words tasted sour.
That night she lay awake. Why did she care so much? She didn't even like piano. What she loved was running. She was the fastest in class, but nobody filmed that.
The next week she asked the PE teacher about the district race and started training on the hill behind her building every morning. When Ines said, "Good luck at your race," Wanjiru blushed and said, "Your concert was really good."

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru train every morning?
qa.a: On the hill behind her building.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru feel about the praise for Ines?
qa.a: Envious and invisible, and her unkind words tasted sour afterwards.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru's envy show her, and how did she use it?
qa.a: It showed she wanted recognition for something she loves, so she began training for the district race.

qa.q: How might Ines have felt hearing Wanjiru's compliment?
qa.a: Pleased and warm, since she had wished Wanjiru good luck too.

grounding: A girl envious of a praised classmate sees what she herself cares about and works on her own strength instead of running the classmate down.
